learningObjectives.title: Rates of reaction and collision theory
Measuring and calculating rates of reaction

questions.q: According to collision theory, for a reaction to occur, particles must collide with:
options: Any speed and any direction
Sufficient energy and the correct orientation
Low energy and no particular orientation
Equal masses and the same charge
questions.explain: A successful (reacting) collision requires both enough energy to break bonds and the correct orientation of the particles.

questions.q: The minimum amount of energy that colliding particles must have in order to react is called the:
options: Activation energy
Kinetic energy
Ionisation energy
Bond energy
questions.explain: Activation energy is the minimum energy particles need to collide successfully and react.

questions.q: Which of the following will increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: Lowering the temperature
Increasing the temperature
Using larger lumps of a solid reactant
Decreasing the concentration of a reactant
questions.explain: Raising the temperature gives particles more energy so collisions are more frequent and more energetic, increasing the rate.

questions.q: Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of reaction?
options: Particles gain mass and collide harder
Particles move faster, so they collide more frequently and with more energy
The activation energy of the reaction falls
Fewer particles are present so collisions are cleaner
questions.explain: Higher temperature increases particle kinetic energy, raising both the frequency and energy of collisions.

questions.q: A catalyst is a substance that:
options: Speeds up a reaction and is used up in the process
Slows down a reaction and is not changed
Speeds up a reaction without being used up
Changes the products formed in a reaction
questions.explain: A catalyst increases the rate of reaction but is not used up, so it can be reused.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It increases the temperature of the reactants
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the concentration of the reactants
It raises the activation energy needed to react
questions.explain: A catalyst offers a route with lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

questions.q: Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increases the rate of reaction because:
options: There are more reactant particles in a given volume, so collisions are more frequent
The particles have more energy per collision
The activation energy is lowered
The particles move more slowly and collide gently
questions.explain: Higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, giving a greater frequency of collisions.

questions.q: A powdered solid reacts faster than the same mass of large lumps because the powder has:
options: A lower activation energy
A greater surface area, allowing more frequent collisions
More energetic particles
A higher concentration
questions.explain: Breaking a solid into a powder exposes more surface area, so more collisions occur per second.

questions.q: For a reaction between gases, increasing the pressure increases the rate because:
options: The gas particles gain more energy
The gas particles are pushed closer together, increasing collision frequency
The activation energy is reduced
The temperature always rises with pressure
questions.explain: Higher pressure squeezes gas particles into a smaller volume, so they collide more often.

questions.q: On a graph of volume of gas produced against time for two reactions, the steeper line indicates:
options: A slower reaction
A faster reaction
A reaction that has stopped
A reversible reaction
questions.explain: A steeper gradient means product is being formed more quickly, so the rate is faster.

questions.q: For a typical reaction, how does the rate change as the reaction proceeds?
options: It stays constant until the reaction suddenly stops
It is fastest at the start and slows as reactants are used up
It is slowest at the start and speeds up over time
It increases steadily until all reactants are gone
questions.explain: Reactant concentration is highest at the start, so the rate is greatest then and falls as reactants deplete.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus is commonly used to measure the volume of gas produced in a reaction over time?
options: A thermometer
A gas syringe
A measuring cylinder of solid
A voltmeter
questions.explain: A gas syringe collects and measures the volume of gas released as the reaction proceeds.

questions.q: A reaction produces 48 cm3 of gas in 24 seconds. What is the mean rate of reaction?
options: 2 cm3/s
24 cm3/s
72 cm3/s
questions.explain: Mean rate = volume of gas / time = 48 cm3 / 24 s = 2 cm3/s.

questions.q: In the 'disappearing cross' experiment, sodium thiosulfate reacts with acid and the rate is followed by measuring:
options: The mass of gas lost from the flask
The time taken for a cloudy precipitate to hide a cross viewed through the flask
The temperature rise of the solution
The colour change from blue to colourless
questions.explain: The reaction forms a sulfur precipitate that turns the mixture cloudy, obscuring the cross; a shorter time means a faster rate.

questions.q: In a reaction that gives off a gas, why does the mass of the reaction flask decrease when measured on a balance?
options: The reactants are destroyed
Gas escapes from the flask, reducing the total mass
The balance gains energy from the reaction
Water evaporates from the solid reactant
questions.explain: As gas leaves the open flask, the measured mass falls, and the loss can be used to follow the rate.

questions.q: Which symbol is used in an equation to show that a reaction is reversible?
questions.explain: The double half-arrow ⇌ shows that a reaction can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions.

questions.q: Dynamic equilibrium in a reversible reaction can only be reached in a:
options: Closed system
Open beaker
System at absolute zero
System with no reactants
questions.explain: A closed system prevents reactants or products escaping, allowing forward and reverse reactions to balance.

questions.q: At dynamic equilibrium, which statement is correct?
options: Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
There are no reactants left, only products
The reactant and product concentrations are always equal
questions.explain: At equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.

questions.q: In the Haber process, N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards:
options: The reactants, because they have more molecules
The products (ammonia), the side with fewer gas molecules
Neither side, as pressure has no effect
The side with more gas molecules
questions.explain: Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules; the right has 2 moles versus 4 on the left, so more ammonia forms.

questions.q: For a reversible reaction at equilibrium, increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the direction that is:
options: Exothermic
Endothermic
Always towards the products
Unchanged by temperature
questions.explain: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat energy.
